newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says 1997 German deficit to meet EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says 1997 German deficit to meet EMU goal.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday the country's 1997 public sector budget deficit would beat the target set for European monetary union but urged state and municipal governments to save more cash.

Speaking at talks on public spending at federal, state and local levels, Waigel said the total German deficit would meet his goal of 2.5 percent of gross domestic product as measured under the rules of the Maastricht Treaty.
"A great majority of states and communes are matching the federal government's savings," Waigel told a meeting of the government's financial planning council.

But he felt the federal government was carrying the brunt of the cuts, reducing its spending by 2.5 percent to 440 billion marks ($293.1 billion) -- equal to a record low 12 percent of GDP -- while overall spending by the 16 states would be unchanged.

Germany would still meet Maastricht's deficit target with room to spare, he said, but added: "States and local governments must also make their contribution to lasting growth through a strict savings policy."

Waigel is slugging it out with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) over tax policy. The SPD-controlled Bundesrat has rejected his 1997 tax bill and sent it to parliament's mediation committee which will meet on Thursday.

While SPD states are sore at losing revenues once wealth taxes are abolished, leaders fell into line with Waigel on Europe. The SPD lost votes in regional polls this year when it campaigned against the single currency.
Heinz Schleusser, finance minister in Germany's most populous state North Rhine-Westphalia -- where his SPD governs in coalition with the Green party -- told reporters Maastricht targets must be met.

Both he and Bavaria's conservative finance minister Erwin Huber said Germany must agree an internal stability pact to ensure lasting fiscal prudence once monetary union is in place. "I expect an agreement at the start of 1997," Schleusser said.

Waigel is also seeking a deal among countries taking part in the launch of the Euro currency to impose fines on those failing to control state borrowing, but his initiative has hit resistance from most other European Union members.

His federal deficit goal next year is 53.3 billion marks -- down from 73 billion marks this year. The 1997 figure includes 3.1 billion marks in planned privatisation proceeds, which do not count towards measuring the Maastricht deficit criterion.
And, based on figures Waigel presented to the council, new borrowing by the states will total 37.5 billion marks. Local governments would borrow seven billion more.
Accounting for other factors, the total public deficit will fall 20 billion marks to 99.5 billion, by Waigel's reckoning.
Although Germany hopes to meet the EMU deficit target, total public debt will exceed the Maastricht reference value of 60 percent of GDP, hitting 61 percent next year.
